paragraphs.context: I wrote this book because I’ve always loved the theater.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Why the writer wrote this book.
paragraphs.simple: The writer loves plays. She acted in many plays when she was young, and her husband Will writes and acts in plays. They both love Shakespeare's plays.

background.note: William Shakespeare (1564 to 1616) was an English writer of plays and poems. Many people think he is the greatest writer in English.
Shakespeare's theater in London. A copy of it was built in London in 1997, near the old place.

paragraphs.context: My main research for Stage Fright on a Summer Night, though, comes from my memories of being onstage.
paragraphs.mainIdea: How it feels to be on a stage.
paragraphs.simple: Her best "research" is remembering how it felt to be on a stage: waiting at the side, with your heart beating fast, wet hands and shaking knees. Then it is your turn!

paragraphs.context: While they are gone, no time at all passes in Frog Creek.
paragraphs.simple: The tree house takes them to the places in its books. When they are away, time stops at home, so nobody knows they were gone.

paragraphs.context: Morgan is a magical librarian of Camelot
paragraphs.simple: The tree house belongs to Morgan le Fay, a magic librarian from King Arthur's Camelot. She travels through time to collect books.

background.note: In old stories about King Arthur, Morgan le Fay is a woman who can do magic. In these books she is a kind librarian.
The castle and city of King Arthur in old British stories.

paragraphs.context: In Magic Tree House Books #25–28, Jack and Annie search for special kinds of magic.
paragraphs.simple: In earlier books they helped Morgan and Camelot. Now, in books 25 to 28, they will look for special kinds of magic.

paragraphs.context: Lightning bugs blinked in the warm summer twilight.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie sit outside on a warm summer evening. Small insects make little lights in the dark.

paragraphs.context: The light hovered above the Frog Creek woods.
paragraphs.simple: They see a light go across the sky. It stops over the woods and then goes down into the trees.

paragraphs.context: “Ten minutes, no more!” their mom said.
paragraphs.simple: Their mother says they can go out for ten minutes. (Time stops when they travel, so ten minutes is enough.)

paragraphs.context: A beautiful woman with long white hair stood in the shadowy corner.
paragraphs.simple: When they climb in, they see Morgan le Fay standing in the corner. They hug her.

paragraphs.context: Now I want you to do something good for yourselves. You are going to learn magic.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan says they have helped her and Camelot a lot. Now she wants them to do something good for themselves: learn magic.

paragraphs.context: There is magic that does not need charms or spells
paragraphs.simple: Annie wants to learn spells. But Morgan says some magic does not need spells. They will find a special magic on each of their next four trips.

paragraphs.context: A secret rhyme will guide you on each journey
paragraphs.simple: For each trip, a short poem will help them. Morgan gives them the first one on a small piece of paper.

paragraphs.context: To find a special magic,
paragraphs.simple: The rhyme says: to find a special magic, you must step into the light, and without magic tools or words, make day become night.

paragraphs.context: “Turn daytime into night?” said Jack. “How can we do that?”
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks it is impossible to make day become night. Morgan only smiles and says they must find out.

paragraphs.context: “What’s o-l-d-e mean?” asked Annie.
paragraphs.simple: The book is called "Merry Olde England". Jack says "olde" is an old way to write "old". You say it the same way.

paragraphs.context: The wind blew harder and harder.
paragraphs.simple: The wind blows stronger and stronger, the tree house spins, and then everything stops. They have arrived.

paragraphs.context: Annie was wearing a long dress with an apron.
paragraphs.simple: The magic has given them clothes from 1600. Annie has a long dress and an apron. Jack has a shirt with big round sleeves, short trousers and tights. They both wear soft leather shoes.

paragraphs.context: The tree house had landed in a patch of trees near a wide brown river.
paragraphs.simple: The tree house is in some trees near a wide river. Many people, carts and boats are going toward the river.

paragraphs.context: In 1600, over 100,000 people lived in London, England.
paragraphs.simple: In 1600 more than 100,000 people lived in London. Queen Elizabeth the First ruled England, and her people loved her.

background.note: Queen of England from 1558 to 1603. Her time is called the Elizabethan age.

paragraphs.context: The bridge looked like a small town.
paragraphs.simple: A big stone bridge crosses the river. It has houses, shops and even a church on it, so it looks like a small town.

paragraphs.context: At the heart of London was London Bridge.
paragraphs.mainIdea: What the book says about the bridge.
paragraphs.simple: London Bridge was in the centre of London, over the Thames River. It fell down many times, but people always built it again.

background.note: The big river that goes through London.

paragraphs.context: “That must be where the song comes from.”
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks of the children's song "London Bridge is falling down" and starts to sing it.

background.note: A very old English song for children.

paragraphs.context: “P-U!” Annie said, holding her nose.
paragraphs.simple: "P-U" is what children say when something smells very bad. The river smells terrible.

paragraphs.context: A group of ragged boys brushed past Jack and Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Some boys in old, torn clothes run past. They are about twelve or thirteen. They are laughing and say they will be late.

paragraphs.context: “Late for what?” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie wants to know where the boys are going. She does not want to wait for Jack to read, so she runs after them.

paragraphs.context: The bridge was so noisy and smelly!
paragraphs.simple: The bridge is very noisy and smells bad. Wheels are loud on the stones, horses make noises, and shopkeepers shout what they are selling.

paragraphs.context: A shopkeeper caught Jack’s eye. “What lack you, boy?” he shouted.
paragraphs.simple: A shopkeeper looks at Jack and asks, "What lack you?" This is old English for "What do you need?" He wants Jack to buy something.

paragraphs.context: She pointed to a bear in a wooden cage in the back of the cart.
paragraphs.simple: A cart goes past with a bear in a cage. The bear's fur is dirty and its head is down.

paragraphs.context: She pointed at huge black birds sitting hunched at the edges of the rooftops.
paragraphs.simple: Big black birds sit on the roofs and look down at everyone. Jack feels afraid and walks past quickly.

paragraphs.context: There was no sign of the group of ragged boys.
paragraphs.simple: At the end of the bridge, they look for the older boys, but cannot see them anywhere.

paragraphs.context: London Bridge connected London to the south bank of the river
paragraphs.mainIdea: The south side of the river.
paragraphs.simple: The bridge went to the south side of the river. People went there to have fun. A place called the Bear Garden was popular.

paragraphs.context: I’m getting a bad feeling about the Bear Garden.
paragraphs.simple: When they hear loud shouting from the round building, Annie feels something is wrong. She asks Jack to read more.

paragraphs.context: At an arena called the Bear Garden, people watched bears fight with dogs.
paragraphs.simple: In the Bear Garden, people watched bears fight with dogs. Animal fights were common then, but now they are against the law.

paragraphs.context: “I understand,” Annie said. “You don’t want to fight.
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks the bear is asking her to take him away. She starts to open his cage.

paragraphs.context: “But we can’t just steal him. That guy is his owner.”
paragraphs.simple: Annie wants to save Dan from the bear fights. Jack says they cannot just take him, because he belongs to the man.

paragraphs.context: He needed to get Annie’s mind off the bear.
paragraphs.simple: Jack wants Annie to stop thinking about the bear. He sees the older boys going into a white building and says they should follow them.

paragraphs.context: A PLAY AT THE GLOBE THEATER!
paragraphs.simple: The sign says there is a play at the Globe Theater: A Midsummer Night's Dream. Annie loves plays, so Jack is happy.

paragraphs.context: “A penny to stand! A penny to stand!” he shouted.
paragraphs.simple: A man at the door says it costs only a penny to go in and stand. Jack thinks that is very cheap.

paragraphs.context: “What will you do with him if you free him, Annie?” he asked.
paragraphs.simple: Annie still wants to free the bear. Jack asks what she will do with him. She says she will think of something.

paragraphs.context: Because there was no electricity, plays were performed during the day, when it was light.
paragraphs.simple: There were no electric lights, so plays were in the daytime. Tickets were cheap, so almost everyone could go.

paragraphs.context: Seating for the audience depended on how much was paid.
paragraphs.simple: Rich people paid more and sat in the high seats. Other people paid less and stood near the stage.

paragraphs.context: He was long-legged, with a trim beard and twinkly eyes.
paragraphs.simple: A tall man with a short beard and happy eyes hurries over. He heard Jack read, and he thinks Jack reads very well.

paragraphs.context: “Because I have just lost two fairies!” he said.
paragraphs.simple: The man says he has "lost two fairies". He means two actors who play fairies. Jack thinks he is crazy.

paragraphs.context: “Two boy actors didn’t show up today to play fairies,”
paragraphs.simple: Two boys did not come to act as fairies in the play. The man wants Jack to read both parts.

paragraphs.context: “There are three thousand people here today, waiting to see the play I have written!
paragraphs.simple: The man wrote the play. Three thousand people are waiting to see it, and one of them is the most important person in the world.

paragraphs.context: “Surely you know it’s against the law for girls to go on the stage,”
paragraphs.simple: Annie wants to act, but the man says girls are not allowed on the stage. In Shakespeare's time, boys played all the girls' parts.

paragraphs.context: He will only be in your play if I can be in it, too.
paragraphs.simple: Annie tells the man that Jack will only act if she can act too. Jack quietly says that is not what he wants.

paragraphs.context: You get to read your part. You don’t have to memorize it.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says it will be fun. Jack can read his words from paper. He does not have to learn them.

paragraphs.context: Jack could tell that Annie really, really wanted to be in the play.
paragraphs.simple: Jack sees how much Annie wants to act. And the play will help her stop thinking about the bear. So he says yes.

paragraphs.context: But Annie will have to pretend to be a boy.
paragraphs.simple: The man agrees. Annie must hide her hair and pretend to be a boy called Andy.

paragraphs.context: “My name is Will, by the way,” he said.
paragraphs.simple: The play starts. The man says his name is Will and tells them to be very fast.
paragraphs.tone: A small secret: Will is William Shakespeare, but Jack and Annie do not know it yet.

paragraphs.context: Actors were rushing about everywhere.
paragraphs.simple: In a small room, actors are busy getting ready: putting on capes, tying ropes and saying their words to themselves.

paragraphs.context: It was crammed with fancy gowns, purple and blue capes
paragraphs.simple: The room is full of beautiful dresses, capes, wigs, hats and masks. Annie thinks the masks would be good for hiding who you are.

paragraphs.context: Didn’t she know they were about to stand in front of three thousand people?
paragraphs.simple: Annie is calm, but Jack is very nervous. Thinking about three thousand people makes him sweat, and his stomach feels strange.

paragraphs.context: “Here are your rolls,” he said.
paragraphs.simple: Will gives them each a rolled paper with only their own words on it. Jack sees that he has two long speeches, not just a few lines.

background.note: In Shakespeare's time, each actor got a roll of paper with his words. This is why we now call an actor's part a "role".

paragraphs.context: And above all, act natural.
paragraphs.simple: Will says: speak clearly, with feeling, and act natural. Jack thinks this is impossible when he is so afraid.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Andy, meet Puck, ‘merry wanderer of the night.’
paragraphs.simple: A short, round man in green runs in, very worried. He is the actor who plays Puck, a fairy in the play. Will tells him Jack and Andy can read the parts.

background.note: A funny fairy in A Midsummer Night's Dream who likes to play tricks. He is called "the merry wanderer of the night".

paragraphs.context: A huge crowd stood directly in front of the stage.
paragraphs.simple: Jack sees the stage. Its roof is painted blue with stars and a moon. Many people stand in front of the stage, and more sit above.

paragraphs.context: “I’ll take you onstage first,” Puck whispered to Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Puck tells Jack to start reading when Puck asks, "How now, spirit! Whither wander you?" That means "Hello, fairy! Where are you going?"

paragraphs.context: “You go onstage with the fairy queen,”
paragraphs.simple: Annie will go on with the fairy queen. When the queen asks for a song, Annie must sing. Puck says she can make up the music.

paragraphs.context: “The groundlings get a bit wild,” said Puck.
paragraphs.simple: The "groundlings" are the noisy people who stand near the stage. They sometimes shout rude things or throw old fruit at the actors.

paragraphs.context: That does it, thought Jack.
paragraphs.simple: That is too much for Jack. He feels sick, so he tries to leave. But he meets Will on the stairs.

paragraphs.context: “There is nothing to fear,” Will whispered.
paragraphs.simple: Will tells Jack to close his eyes and imagine he is a fairy in a forest on a summer night, with the moon and owls.

paragraphs.context: Will’s deep whisper seemed to cast a spell over Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Will's quiet voice works like magic. Jack feels calmer and can see the forest in his mind.

paragraphs.context: He opened his mouth. No sound came out.
paragraphs.simple: Puck asks his question, but Jack cannot say anything. Someone in the crowd makes a rude "sss" sound.

paragraphs.context: He felt the summer night. He took a deep breath.
paragraphs.simple: Jack closes his eyes and imagines the summer night. He breathes deeply and gets ready to read.

paragraphs.context: Over hill, over dale
paragraphs.simple: Jack reads the fairy's words from the play: the fairy goes everywhere, over hills and valleys, through plants, water and fire, faster than the moon, and works for the Fairy Queen.

paragraphs.context: As Jack read, the audience grew quiet. Jack forgot he was Jack.
paragraphs.simple: The people become quiet. Jack forgets that he is Jack. He feels that he really is a fairy in the forest.

paragraphs.context: He couldn’t believe he’d just performed, acted, in front of all those people!
paragraphs.simple: Will says Jack was brilliant. Jack's face goes red. He cannot believe he acted in front of so many people, and he even had fun.

paragraphs.context: You spotted snakes, with double tongue,
paragraphs.simple: Annie sings the fairies' song. It tells snakes, hedgehogs and other small animals to go away and not hurt the Fairy Queen.

paragraphs.context: The audience howled with laughter.
paragraphs.simple: Annie acts out the words with her hands and funny faces. She even dances. The people laugh loudly and cheer.

paragraphs.context: It was about people in love. But none were able to marry the people they loved.
paragraphs.simple: Jack watches the play. He cannot understand every word, but he understands the story about people in love.

paragraphs.context: So he put magic juice on her eyelids
paragraphs.simple: The fairy king is angry with the queen. He puts magic juice on her eyes, so she will love the first person she sees.

paragraphs.context: So he put the head of a donkey on a funny man.
paragraphs.simple: Puck puts a donkey's head on a funny man. The queen wakes up, sees him and falls in love with him.

paragraphs.context: “I have had a most rare vision,” he said.
paragraphs.simple: Later the magic ends and the man has his own head again. He says he had a very strange and wonderful dream. Jack likes these words.

paragraphs.context: Jack’s heart started to pound. He had a scary thought
paragraphs.simple: It is almost time to bow, but Annie is not there. Jack is afraid that she has gone to free the bear.

paragraphs.context: So good night unto you all.
paragraphs.simple: Puck says the last words of the play: good night to all of you, and clap if you liked it. ("Give me your hands" means clap.)

paragraphs.context: She has graced us with her presence today.
paragraphs.simple: Will thanks the most important person in the world for coming to the play.

paragraphs.context: Will made a sweeping bow to a woman in a gallery above the stage.
paragraphs.simple: Will bows to a woman in the high seats. She wears a white dress with pearls and covers her face.

paragraphs.context: “Long live Queen Elizabeth!” said Will.
paragraphs.simple: It is Queen Elizabeth! Will and all the people shout "Long live Queen Elizabeth!" to show their love for her.

paragraphs.context: Today, they gave us a special kind of magic—the magic of theater.
paragraphs.simple: The queen says the actors gave everyone the magic of theater: they turned daytime into night. That is the special magic in Morgan's rhyme.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, man,” whispered Jack. That was it—the special magic.
paragraphs.simple: Jack understands: the special magic is theater. They stepped into the light (the bright stage) and, with no magic, made people feel it was night.

paragraphs.context: I put a costume on him. So if we passed people on the way here, they’d think he was an actor.
paragraphs.simple: Annie took the bear and put a cape, a wig and a lion mask on him. People thought he was an actor.

paragraphs.context: “I wasn’t stealing. I was saving,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says she stole the bear. Annie says she saved him. But she does not know what to do with him now.

paragraphs.context: “Thieves!” he yelled. “Give him back! I’m selling him to the fights!”
paragraphs.simple: The owner finds them and shouts. Annie stands in front of the bear and says he is a gentle bear, not a fighter.

paragraphs.context: “ ’Tis, indeed,” said a deep voice.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says bear fighting is stupid. A deep voice says, "It is, really." It is Will, with Puck.

paragraphs.context: “Tut, tut, you’re a sorry sight, man,”
paragraphs.simple: Will tells the owner he looks bad for selling an old, gentle bear to the fights. Will says he wants a bear for a play, so he pays for Dan.

paragraphs.context: Tell the actors they needn’t be afraid of him. He’s tamer than most of them.
paragraphs.simple: Will tells Puck to take the bear to the horses' building. He jokes that the bear is more gentle than most of his actors.

paragraphs.context: “Thank you both for helping me,” said Will. “You saved the day.”
paragraphs.simple: Will says they "saved the day" (helped at the last moment). Jack jokes that they saved the night, because they played fairies in a night forest.

paragraphs.context: The river smelled as bad as before, but Jack didn’t mind now.
paragraphs.simple: The water shows the pink and purple sky. The river still smells bad, but now Jack does not care.

paragraphs.context: “Ah, and I’ll note you both in my book of memory,”
paragraphs.simple: Jack wants to write his memories. Will says he will always remember them too. (These are words from one of Shakespeare's plays.)

paragraphs.context: “Why does Queen Elizabeth have black teeth?”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Why the queen's teeth are black.
paragraphs.simple: Will says she eats too much sugar. He says the queen does not know how she looks, because she has not looked in a good mirror for twenty years.

paragraphs.context: You see, all the world’s a stage.
paragraphs.simple: Will says: the queen pretends to be young, Annie pretended to be a boy, and the bear pretended to be an actor. All the world is like a stage, and people are like actors.

paragraphs.context: “Thy life’s a miracle, isn’t it?” he said.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie tell Will about the tree house. Will smiles and says their life is a wonderful thing.

paragraphs.context: Why don’t you both stay here instead?
paragraphs.simple: Will asks them to stay, live and act at the Globe Theater. He will ask the queen to let Annie act, and he will teach them to write plays.

paragraphs.context: Parting is such sweet sorrow.
paragraphs.simple: Will understands. He says good-bye with famous words: saying good-bye is sad, but also sweet.

paragraphs.context: At that moment, Jack did feel sweet sorrow.
paragraphs.simple: Jack feels the same sad and sweet feeling. He wants to stay a little longer, but Annie makes the wish to go home.

paragraphs.context: He and Annie took out the two scrolls Will had given them.
paragraphs.simple: At home they open the scrolls. Will has written his name on them. (The name is a picture in the book.)

paragraphs.context: William Shakespeare lived from 1564 to 1616.
paragraphs.simple: The book says William Shakespeare wrote 37 plays and many poems. Many people think he was the greatest writer ever.

paragraphs.context: He stared in amazement at William Shakespeare’s autograph.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie understand: their friend Will was William Shakespeare! Jack is amazed.

paragraphs.context: Then he took a deep breath and spoke very clearly and with feeling:
paragraphs.simple: Walking home, they remember the play. Jack says the famous line from the play clearly and with feeling, as Will taught him.

paragraphs.context: William Shakespeare did write a play that included a small part for a bear.
paragraphs.simple: Shakespeare really wrote a play with a small part for a bear. It is called The Winter's Tale.

paragraphs.context: Queen Elizabeth’s teeth were black from eating too much sugar
paragraphs.simple: The queen's teeth really were black from sugar. One of her helpers wrote that for twenty years nobody gave her a good mirror.

paragraphs.context: There is no historical evidence that Queen Elizabeth I ever visited the Globe Theater.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Did the queen go to the Globe?
paragraphs.simple: We do not know that the queen ever went to the Globe. But she liked Shakespeare's plays, and A Midsummer Night's Dream was probably shown at her palace.

paragraphs.context: That’s because in Shakespeare’s time, people dropped their admission money into a box
paragraphs.simple: People put their money in a box at the door, so today the ticket office is called a "box office".

paragraphs.context: The reason actors’ parts are now called “roles”
paragraphs.simple: Actors got rolls of paper with their words. That is why a part in a play is now called a "role".

paragraphs.context: For over 400 years, people have been quoting lines written by Shakespeare.
paragraphs.simple: People still use Shakespeare's words today. The next lines show where the words in this book come from.

paragraphs.context: It is believed that William Shakespeare invented over 2,000 words and expressions
paragraphs.simple: Shakespeare probably made up more than 2,000 words and expressions that we still use. The list of these words from the story is not shown here. It has words like "lonely", "excitement", "gloomy", "upstairs", "downstairs", "good riddance" and "swift as a shadow".

sentences.grammar: "To make her ..." gives the reason. "Make someone do something" (no "to" before "fall").

sentences.context: I put a costume on him. So if we passed people on the way here, they’d think he was an actor.
sentences.simple: I dressed him in a costume, so people would think he was an actor.
sentences.main: They’d think he was an actor.

parts.text: I put a costume on him.
parts.meaning: I dressed him in a costume.

parts.text: So if we passed people on the way here,
parts.meaning: So if we met people while coming here,

parts.text: they’d think he was an actor.
parts.meaning: they would believe he was an actor.

sentences.grammar: "They'd" = they would. "If ... passed, ... would think" talks about what might happen.

sentences.context: I’ll ask the queen to exclude you from the law about girls going onstage, Annie—because of your great talent.
sentences.simple: Will says he will ask the queen to let Annie act, because she is so good at it.

parts.text: I’ll ask the queen
parts.meaning: I will ask the queen

parts.text: to exclude you from the law about girls going onstage,
parts.meaning: to say the law does not stop you from acting,

parts.text: Annie—because of your great talent.
parts.meaning: Annie, because you act so well.

sentences.main: William Shakespeare lived.

sentences.grammar: "From ... to ..." gives the start and the end of a time.

a bit.example: The groundlings get a bit wild

a sorry sight.meaning: Someone or something that looks bad or sad.

act natural.meaning: To behave in your usual way, so no one sees that you are nervous.

against the law.example: They are against the law today.

all my best.meaning: A friendly way to end a letter, like "Best wishes".

all the world's a stage.meaning: Words from Shakespeare: life is like a play, and all people are like actors in it.

along the way.meaning: While doing something; during a trip or a time.
along the way.example: Along the way, Jack and Annie discovered that the tree house belongs to Morgan le Fay.

as if.meaning: In a way that makes you think that something is true.
as if.example: as if they were going someplace fun.

be about to.meaning: To be going to do something very soon.
be about to.example: they were about to stand in front of three thousand people?

be gone.example: So take this money for him and be gone.

before one knew it.meaning: Very quickly, before you could think.
before one knew it.example: Before he knew it, Jack was onstage!

box office.meaning: The place in a theater where people buy tickets.
box office.example: the place where theaters sell tickets is called a “box office.”

break in.meaning: To start talking when someone else is talking.

break into a sweat.meaning: To suddenly start to sweat, because you are afraid or nervous.
break into a sweat.example: The thought made him break into a sweat.

break the spell.meaning: To stop the magic of a spell.
break the spell.example: The fairy king finally broke the spell.

brush past.meaning: To walk past someone so close that you touch them a little.
brush past.example: A group of ragged boys brushed past Jack and Annie.

bump into.meaning: To hit someone by accident while moving.

burst into.meaning: To come into a room suddenly and fast.
burst into.example: a short, chubby man burst into the costume room.

by the way.meaning: You say this when you add something new to the talk.
by the way.example: “My name is Will, by the way,”

cast a spell.meaning: To use magic to change someone. "Cast a spell over Jack" means it worked like magic on Jack.
cast a spell.example: Will’s deep whisper seemed to cast a spell over Jack.

catch one's breath.meaning: To stop breathing for a moment because you are surprised or excited.

catch sight of.example: Then he caught sight of Jack.

catch someone's eye.meaning: To make someone look at you.

clear one's throat.meaning: To cough a little before you speak.

come up.meaning: To come soon; to be next.

dig through.meaning: To look for something among many things.
dig through.example: As Will dug through a large basket of clothes

drown out.meaning: To be so loud that another sound cannot be heard.
drown out.example: His voice was nearly drowned out

fall down.example: At different times in history, the bridge fell down.

fall in love.example: to make her fall in love with the first person she saw.

fall to one's knees.meaning: To go down on your knees suddenly, to show great respect.
fall to one's knees.example: They all fell to their knees.

figure out.meaning: To think about something until you find the answer.
figure out.example: We can figure that out later

find out.meaning: To learn something that you did not know.
find out.example: That’s what you have to find out

for goodness sakes.meaning: A thing that people say when they are worried or angry.

get someone's mind off.meaning: To make someone stop thinking about something.
get someone's mind off.example: He needed to get Annie’s mind off the bear.

get to.meaning: To be allowed to; to have the chance to.
get to.example: You get to read your part.

give a big hand.meaning: To clap for someone for a long time.
give a big hand.example: The audience gave a big hand.

go on.meaning: 1. In a theater: to walk onto the stage. 2. To happen ("What's going on?" = "What is happening?").
go on.example: Actors stood silently nearby, waiting to go on.

good riddance.meaning: You say it when you are happy that someone bad has gone.

grow up.meaning: To change from a child into an adult.
grow up.example: When I was growing up, I performed in many plays.

grow used to.meaning: To slowly get to like or accept something.
grow used to.example: He had grown used to it.

harder and harder.example: The wind blew harder and harder.

heart attack.meaning: When the heart suddenly stops working well. Jack means he is very, very afraid.
heart attack.example: about to have a heart attack?

hold up.meaning: To lift something so people can see it.
hold up.example: She held up a slip of paper.

in a hurry.meaning: Wanting to go or do something very fast.
in a hurry.example: Why are they in such a hurry to get there?

in great need of.example: I am in great need of a boy who is a brilliant reader!

in the wings.meaning: At the side of a stage, where actors wait before they go on.

in time.meaning: Not late. "Just in time to see" means at the last moment, so he could still see it.
in time.example: just in time to see a streak of light

jump in.meaning: To start to talk suddenly, to help someone.

keep going.meaning: To go on; not to stop.

lady in waiting.meaning: A woman who lives with a queen and helps her.
lady in waiting.example: One of the queen’s ladies-in-waiting wrote that

let out.example: He let out a low moan.

light up.example: a flash lit up the tree house.

lightning bug.meaning: A small insect whose body gives out light at night; a firefly.
lightning bug.example: Lightning bugs blinked in the warm summer twilight.

long live.meaning: A way to say "We hope the king or queen lives a long time." People shout it to show love for a king or queen.

look over one's shoulder.meaning: To turn your head and look behind you.

look up.meaning: 1. To raise your eyes and look at something. 2. To find a word or name in a book.
look up.example: Jack looked up at London Bridge as they passed by.

make up.meaning: To make a new song or story from your own ideas.

no longer.example: The scary black birds were no longer on the rooftops.

no sign of.meaning: You cannot see someone or something anywhere.
no sign of.example: There was no sign of the group of ragged boys.

no way.example: “No. No way. I can’t do that,”

once again.example: they all bowed once … twice … and once again.

out of breath.meaning: Breathing fast because you have been running.
out of breath.example: They were laughing and out of breath.

out of the way.meaning: To a place where something will not hit you or stop you.
out of the way.example: He pulled her out of the way.

parting is such sweet sorrow.meaning: Words from Shakespeare: saying good-bye is sad, but sweet too, because you love the person.

past the wit of man.meaning: More than people can understand. (Old English.)
past the wit of man.example: a dream past the wit of man to say what dream it was.

pull aside.meaning: To take someone a little away from other people, to talk to them.

put away.meaning: To put something back in its place.

put on.meaning: To dress yourself in clothes; or to show a play to people.
put on.example: friends in England who put on plays by Shakespeare

raise one's eyebrows.meaning: To move your eyebrows up, because you are surprised.

right now.example: Right now, let’s learn something about this play.

rush about.meaning: To move quickly in many directions.

save the day.meaning: To stop something bad from happening at the last moment.

see you around.meaning: A friendly way to say good-bye.

shooting star.meaning: A small piece of rock from space that burns as it falls, so you see a quick line of light in the night sky.

show up.meaning: To come to a place where people are waiting for you.
show up.example: Two boy actors didn’t show up today

slip away.meaning: To leave quietly so no one sees you.

stage fright.meaning: Fear of being on a stage in front of people.

suck in one's breath.meaning: To breathe in fast because you are surprised or worried.

take a deep breath.meaning: To breathe in a lot of air, often to make yourself calm.

take off.meaning: To leave quickly; to start running.

take out.meaning: To take something out of a bag or a pocket.
take out.example: Jack took out his notebook and wrote:

talk someone into.meaning: To make someone do something by talking to them.
talk someone into.example: How did I let Annie talk me into this?

thin out.example: The theater crowd was thinning out.

throw one's arms around.meaning: To hug someone quickly and strongly.
throw one's arms around.example: They threw their arms around her.

throw up.meaning: To be sick; to bring food up from your stomach through your mouth.
throw up.example: not when he was about to throw up!

tie up.meaning: To tie a boat to something so it stays there.

time and space.example: She travels through time and space, gathering books.

too happy for words.meaning: So happy that you cannot say anything.
too happy for words.example: He was too happy for words.

turn on one's heels.meaning: To turn around quickly and walk away.
turn on one's heels.example: Then Will turned on his heels

under one's breath.meaning: Very quietly, so that only someone near you can hear.

wait a second.meaning: Wait a moment! (You say it when you suddenly see a problem.)

watch out.meaning: Be careful! (You say it when there may be danger.)

what lack you.meaning: What do you need? (Old English. A shopkeeper says it to ask what you want to buy.)

oh man.meaning: "Oh, man" is something you say when you are very surprised or excited. (Friendly talk.) It is not about a real man.
